meeting_header: Date: 2025-11-12 | Start: 14:30 UTC | Duration: 57m | Attendees: Sophie Tan, Liam O'Connor, Jasper Nguyen (Redwood) — Maria Lopez, Daniel Park, Aisha Rahman, Evan Chu (Sable Finance)
summary: Security-focused sync to confirm what admin activity and audit telemetry Redwood captures, export and retention options, and how KMS / key rotation fits into Sable Finance's compliance controls. Agreed to share SOC 2 artifacts, KMS diagrams, and run a focused export benchmark next week.
topics: What events are captured (admin actions, API calls, model usage metadata)
Export formats and destinations (JSONL, Parquet, streaming to S3 / private bucket)
KMS integration, customer keys vs Redwood-managed keys, key rotation
Audit log immutability, tamper-evidence, and chain-of-custody
Operational playbooks for incident response and e-discovery
transcript:
[00:00] Sophie Tan: Hi everyone thanks for joining, we have about 57 minutes on the calendar. Quick intros?
[00:10] Maria Lopez: Maria here, head of security at Sable. We'll mostly focus on audit capture and key rotation.
[00:22] Liam O'Connor: Liam from Redwood, I lead security integrations — I'll cover KMS and export pipelines.
[00:32] Daniel Park: Daniel, platform engineer, we operate Sable's cloud infra and handle storage destinations.
[00:40] Aisha Rahman: Aisha, GRC, will drive the retention and legal hold requirements.
[00:48] Sophie: Great, high-level agenda: what telemetry Redwood records for admin activity, how you can export it, retention options, and KMS/key rotation patterns. We'll leave time at the end for follow-ups.
[01:05] Liam: I'll kick off with the event types — so Redwood captures admin console actions (user create/delete, role changes), API-level actions (token creation, model pinning), and system-level events like autoscale triggers. We also surface per-request metadata: model id, model variant, timestamp, requester id, route, and token counts.
[01:35] Daniel: Is usage metadata tied back to user identity or service accounts? We need to correlate with our internal IAM.
[01:44] Liam: Yes, all events include actor (OIDC or SAML sub), source_ip, and optional request headers. Small caveat — sometimes the auth principal is surfaced as an internal id if the token was created by Redwood for a customer-owned key, so mapping may need an internal lookup.
[02:05] Maria: We care about immutable audit trails — can logs be tamper-evident?
[02:12] Liam: We support append-only exports and sign the export bundles with server-side keys. For higher assurance you can stream to your cloud bucket (we support S3/GCS/Azure Blob) using write-once lifecycle rules on your side; Redwood will push via secure endpoint. We can also send a concurrent signed hash chain if you want cryptographic chain-of-custody.
[02:42] Aisha: How granular are the admin events — do you capture policy changes, RBAC role edits, and delegated admin actions?
[02:50] Sophie: Yep — role grants, permission edits, OAuth client creations, SSO config changes — all captured with before/after diffs where applicable. Sometimes diffs are truncated for very large objects but a pointer to the full payload is included.
[03:10] Evan Chu: Does audit logging include model prompt/response payloads?
[03:17] Liam: By default we do not capture full prompt/response text for privacy reasons. We capture metadata (token counts, model id, completion status). If you need payload capture for incident investigations you can opt-in per-route and specify a retention policy; we recommend encrypting those payload exports with your KMS keys.
[03:40] Daniel: Regarding exports — what formats are available and is there streaming vs batch?
[03:45] Liam: Two primary modes: streaming (near real-time) to a destination via secure channel, usually JSONL; or periodic batch exports (Parquet preferred for analytics). Streaming has sub-second latency and is ideal for SIEM ingestion. Batch exports are compact and schema-evolved for long term storage.
[04:10] Maria: We need records kept for 7 years for some product lines. Can Redwood guarantee retention on its side?
[04:18] Sophie: Redwood maintains short-term retention (90/180/365 days configurable depending on plan). For long-term you should export to your own storage — Redwood provides export APIs and lifecycle hooks. For Dedicated/Private deployments we can extend on-platform retention with contracts, but generally long-term archival is customer-managed.
[04:42] Aisha: What about legal holds or e-discovery: can we lock exports from deletion?
[04:48] Liam: We expose an export locking feature: when you request a legal hold we create an immutable snapshot and hold it from rotation; snapshots can be pushed to your bucket with write-once policies. On-hosted plans we do a time-limited hold and provide verifiable proofs; for Private deployments you control the retention entirely.
[05:15] Daniel: KMS — we run keys in our HSM via AWS KMS. How do you integrate?
[05:22] Liam: Two options: 1) Redwood-managed encryption where Redwood manages a KMS key and encrypts at rest, we rotate keys per our schedule and provide rotation logs; 2) Customer-managed keys (CMKs) where you grant Redwood encrypt/decrypt permissions for a key in your account (cross-account role). For highest control we recommend CMKs with envelope encryption — Redwood stores wrapped data keys; master keys stay in your KMS.
[05:55] Maria: Key rotation is a big area — if we rotate keys monthly, what does that do to existing audit archives? Are old exports still readable?
[06:03] Liam: With envelope encryption we re-wrap the data-key under the new master key when you rotate, or we keep historical wrapped keys so old archives remain decryptable. We can also store key version metadata in the export manifest so you can apply the correct key during restore. That manifest is part of the bundle and is signed.
[06:30] Sophie: Quick note — in some hosted cases customers request Redwood to hold keys for operational reasons; we recommend CMK for compliance.
[06:42] Aisha: For our compliance docs we need step-by-step key rotation procedures showing no downtime.
[06:48] Liam: We'll send a sample rotation playbook. It includes: schedule, re-wrapping steps, export manifest verification, and rollback. We can demo this in a 30m runbook session.
[07:05] Maria: Are admin events exported with user agent and IP — we need to correlate suspicious sessions to geo.
[07:12] Liam: Yes, source_ip, geo (inferred), user_agent, and a request_trace id to join across services.
[07:25] Daniel: If we push streaming to our SIEM, how do you handle backpressure?
[07:31] Liam: We buffer and apply persistent queues. If your endpoint becomes unavailable Redwood will retry with exponential backoff and provide dead-letter buckets. We also support webhook ack semantics so you can control commit.
[07:50] Evan: Do you support signed S3 uploads (pre-signed) from the agent to our bucket so Redwood doesn't hold credentials?
[07:56] Liam: Yes — pre-signed uploads are supported for batch exports, and for streaming we can create a short-lived upload session. For CMK workflows the wrapped key is uploaded alongside the bundle.
[08:12] Maria: About scope — are model fine-tuning operations, manual moderation actions, and reranks captured?
[08:20] Sophie: All administrative model lifecycle events (upload, fine-tune start/stop, policy overrides) and content moderation adjudications are logged as admin events; sensitive payloads can be excluded unless explicitly opted-in.
[08:40] Aisha: We must demonstrate separation of duties — can you show audit trails that distinguish who approved model access vs who deployed?
[08:46] Liam: Events include actor role and whether the action was performed via UI or API, plus a change diff. That helps show separation of duties.
[08:58] Maria: For SOC 2 we need evidence around monitoring — does Redwood keep tamper logs and integrity checks?
[09:05] Liam: Internally we have immutable storage and WORM policies for certain artifacts; externally we provide signed manifests and hash chains for exported bundles. We'll include a short note on how we derive integrity proofs in the artifacts we send.
[09:28] Daniel: Is there RBAC integration with our existing SAML groups so logs reference our roles?
[09:34] Liam: Yes — you can map SAML group attributes to Redwood roles and group membership is included in the event payload.
[09:42] Sophie: Quick interjection — sometimes the auto-transcript may show 'KV cash' instead of KV cache, ignore that — we track KV cache hits for model context reuse.
[09:56] Daniel (laughing): Noted.
[10:03] Evan: On retention settings, can we set a per-route retention? For example: requests to /sensitive-model keep 30 days, other routes 365?
[10:12] Liam: Yes, routing-level retention profiles are supported. You can pin routes to a retention and an export cadence, and those are shown in the export manifest.
[10:30] Maria: For data residency — can we require that export endpoints live in eu-west-1?
[10:36] Sophie: Absolutely, for hosted plans we support region-specific export endpoints. For private deployments you fully control the region. We'll document the available regions and endpoints.
[10:50] Aisha: How about SIEM parsing — do you provide a schema or mapping for common SIEMs?
[10:56] Liam: We provide a canonical schema and connectors for Splunk, Sumo, Datadog, and generic S3 ingestion. Schema evolves; we version the event schema and include a compatibility matrix in the export bundle.
[11:18] Daniel: Are there any rate limits on audit export throughput? We ingest a lot — spikes during deployments may create big volumes.
[11:26] Liam: We have tiered throughput limits; for high-volume customers we recommend dedicated export pipelines via Dedicated capacity or private setup with a direct peering link. We can provision burst capacity during known rollout windows.
[11:45] Maria: For legal holds, does Redwood support tagging a sequence of events as subject to hold across rolling exports?
[11:52] Liam: Yes — tag-based holds are supported. When you tag an entity we annotate subsequent exports until the hold is released, and the bundle manifests reflect hold metadata.
[12:08] Sophie: We'll pause here for a quick demo — Liam do you want to show the export manifest sample?
[12:14] Liam: Sure, I'm going to share my screen — (screen share noise) — the manifest includes: bundle_id, time_window, schema_version, encryption: {key_id, wrap_algo}, events_count, holds. Note: transcript may transcribe the screen share noise as 'encryption curly braces' — ignore.
[13:00] [screen share walkthrough with occasional crosstalk]
[18:20] Maria: That manifest looks good — can you demonstrate decrypting a historical bundle if keys rotated?
[18:28] Liam: Yes — we have a restore flow. The manifest lists the key version and we either re-wrap or provide the historical wrapped-key in your bucket under restricted ACLs.
[19:05] Daniel: Can we run a short export benchmark to measure latency and bundle sizes?
[19:12] Sophie: Yes — we should schedule that; agreed in next steps.
[19:25] Evan: On compliance evidence — does Redwood provide a timeline of configuration changes? We want a change history for SSO configs and RBAC edits.
[19:33] Liam: That's included as admin-events with before/after and actor metadata, plus an audit-ID to tie related changes together.
[20:00] Maria: Is there an API to query exports programmatically for e-discovery?
[20:07] Liam: Yes — export API supports query by time window, actor, event type, and retention tag. Query returns manifest and pre-signed URL to the bundle.
[20:25] Aisha: For encryption-at-rest, is envelope encryption used for all exports or only when CMK selected?
[20:33] Liam: Envelope encryption is our recommended pattern and is used for exports even if Redwood manages keys; for CMK you retain the master key control.
[20:48] Sophie: A quick clarification: when customers choose Redwood-managed keys we still provide export manifest with key rotation metadata but you won't have access to the master key itself.
[21:02] Maria: For our auditors we need controls around who can request exports — can we gate exports behind approvals?
[21:08] Liam: Yes — export requests can be gated by role and an approvals workflow. For extra assurance exports can be configured to require dual sign-off.
[21:24] Daniel: If an engineer accidentally requests a full payload export, is there a way to cancel before it leaves Redwood?
[21:31] Liam: There's a short window where you can cancel pending exports; we also have pre-export validation hooks to prevent accidental full payload captures unless explicitly allowed.
[21:48] Evan: About metadata naming — will events include our internal project ids? We need to map them.
[21:55] Liam: You can pass custom labels/tags on requests which appear in the event payload; we advise using a consistent tag scheme.
[22:12] Maria: Threat model question — if someone gains access to a Redwood admin account, can they backfill or delete audit events?
[22:20] Liam: We have protections: admin deletions are logged and require high-level privileges; offline snapshots are pushed to customer buckets you control; and for Dedicated/Private deployments you can restrict deletion via policy. We also recommend separation-of-duties and use of customer-managed keys to minimize blast radius.
[22:48] Aisha: For pen tests, do you provide test data sets or helper scripts to validate export integrity?
[22:55] Liam: Yes — we provide a pen-test package including a sample manifest, verification scripts for signed bundles, and a checklist for auditors.
[23:10] Sophie: We'll include the pen-test package in the artifact we share.
[23:20] [longer section discussing network controls and peering; timestamps clipped]
[34:45] Daniel: About retention enforcement if we have multiple teams with different retention requirements, can the policy be hierarchical?
[34:52] Liam: Policies are evaluated by specificity: route-level overrides team-level which overrides org-level. There's also a policy simulator to preview effective retention.
[35:10] Maria: For export verification, do you provide signed timestamps? We need trusted time from an NTP chain.
[35:18] Liam: We include RFC-3161- style timestamps and sign them.
[35:30] Evan: Slight question — can you redact PII in exported bundles automatically?
[35:36] Liam: Redwood supports field-level redaction pipelines; you can supply a redaction config or use our built-in detectors. Redaction is applied prior to encryption so manifests will indicate redaction was performed.
[36:00] Aisha: For our legal team we need a sample export manifest and a sample flagged redaction entry — please include.
[36:06] Sophie: Noted.
[36:20] [participants discuss SLA and log delivery guarantees, some crosstalk]
[42:10] Maria: Any constraints around cross-region exports and encryption compliance? For example, can key material remain in eu while bundle stored in us?
[42:20] Liam: For CMK you control where keys live. We support cross-region replication but for compliance we recommend keeping master keys in the same jurisdiction as critical data. We'll add guidance by region in the doc pack.
[42:50] Daniel: Are there costs for export throughput we should budget for?
[42:56] Sophie: Exporting large volumes has egress and processing costs; we'll include a cost estimate template in the artifact. Dedicated/Private may change cost patterns.
[43:20] Evan: One more ops question — do you preserve original event IDs so we can do dedupe on ingestion side?
[43:28] Liam: Yes — each event has a stable event_id and an export sequence id to help dedupe and ordering.
[43:40] Maria: For SOC 2 evidence, do you provide attestation that exports were generated and delivered on certain dates?
[43:47] Liam: The signed manifest and timestamped delivery receipts serve as attestation; we'll include sample receipts.
[44:05] Sophie: Let's move to the wrap-up and decisions.
[44:12] Maria: Confirmed — we will not enable full payload capture by default. We'll test a small payload capture for incident response only.
[44:22] Aisha: We want monthly key rotations with a documented playbook and audit trail.
[44:30] Daniel: We'll supply our retention matrix and sample S3 bucket config.
[44:36] Sophie: Redwood will share SOC 2/ISO artifacts, the KMS integration diagram, sample rotation playbook, the pen-test package, and the export manifest examples.
[44:50] Liam: I'll own the KMS diagram and playbook.
[45:00] Maria: Let's lock a date for the SE-run export benchmark — 2025-11-19 at 14:00 UTC works for us.
[45:08] Sophie: Great — I'll send calendar invite and include a short pre-req checklist.
[45:16] [short discussion about attendee invitees and scope of the bench]
[46:00] Evan: Two quick clarifications — will Redwood store the historical wrapped-key metadata in the manifest rather than a separate DB?
[46:08] Liam: Yes, manifest holds key_version references and a link to the wrapped-key blob in the bundle.
[46:25] Maria: Any regulatory surprise we should expect?
[46:30] Sophie: Nothing unusual — data residency and key control are the main levers. If you need FedRAMP-like controls that's a different conversation.
[46:45] Aisha: One last ask — include sample SIEM parsers and a Grok/Regex example.
[46:51] Liam: Copy that, will include.
[47:05] Sophie: Ok final recap: deliverables and who owns them, schedule benchmark for 11/19. Anything else?
[47:14] Maria: No, that's it. Thanks.
[47:18] Daniel: Thanks everyone.
[47:22] Sophie: Meeting adjourned. We'll follow up with the doc pack and invite.
[47:30] [end of recording — transcript may miss micro-pauses and filler words.]
